name: Heliotherapy sunlamp

card.summary: Old-style home UV sunlamps, once sold for tanning and skin therapy, now studied mainly for their link to skin cancer.
card.note: Studies of sunbed and sunlamp use have examined melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma risk; unfiltered high-pressure bulbs can emit harmful UVC.

quick.overview:
A sunlamp is a lamp that emits ultraviolet light to tan the skin or to treat skin conditions. Early home models of the 1920s emitted a lot of UVB and were known to burn, and interest in them in looksmaxxing circles is part of the broader tan-gear category.

Today most tanning is done with beds or booths, while sunlamp-type fluorescent tubes and high-pressure bulbs survive as replacement lamps and in medical phototherapy for conditions such as psoriasis.
quick.mechanism: Low-pressure fluorescent lamps use phosphors and glass that filter out UVC, while high-pressure quartz bulbs need a dichroic filter glass to block UVC and UVB. UVA darkens existing pigment and UVB triggers new melanin production.
quick.risks: Epidemiological studies have examined sunbed and sunlamp use in relation to melanoma and skin cancers, and UV radiation is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen. Unfiltered high-pressure bulbs can emit dangerous UVC, and broken lamps release mercury.

lead: A sunlamp is an electric lamp that emits ultraviolet (UV) radiation, used for cosmetic tanning and, in clinical form, for phototherapy of skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema and vitiligo.[1] The term heliotherapy, literally sun treatment, historically referred to using sunlight or its artificial equivalent for therapy; Wikipedia traces sun treatment to ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome.[11]

For appearance, the sunlamp is the root of the indoor-tanning tradition: people use UV lamps to darken the skin because a tan reads as healthier or more attractive, and tan-focused looksmaxxing discussion treats UV lamps as a relative of beds, booths and sunless products. Wikipedia places the fashion for tanned skin in the 1920s, when Coco Chanel's 1923 tan helped popularise it and physicians promoted home sunlamps as sun cures.[2]

Types include low-pressure fluorescent tubes and high-pressure quartz bulbs, typically rated from 250 to 2,000 watts, of which a 400-watt version has been used as a face tanner.[1] Home sunlamps of the 1920s emitted a large share of UVB and often caused burns, a problem later beds addressed by shifting output toward UVA.[2]

Epidemiological studies have examined the relationship between sunbed and sunlamp use and cutaneous malignant melanoma, and UV exposure more broadly is linked with skin cancers.[3][4][5] No published trials have tested sunlamps as an appearance intervention beyond the tan itself.

Public-health bodies take a different view of the same devices. The World Health Organization's IARC classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, and meta-analyses report higher melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer rates among indoor tanners, with the greatest relative increases for those who start young.[2][13] In the clinic, supervised UVB lamps remain an established treatment for psoriasis and other conditions.[11][6]

paras: Low-pressure lamps are fluorescent tubes coated with phosphors, and the glass blocks all UVC. Common sizes run from 80 to 200 watts. High-pressure bulbs are quartz and require purple dichroic filter glass to block UVC and UVB; without it they produce dangerous UVC, which is illegal in a salon setting.[1]

Older choke ballasts and newer electronic ballasts power the lamps, the latter being more efficient but costing three to five times more per lamp.[1] Output is described as peaking when the unit is between about 32 and 43 degrees Celsius.[1]
Early lamps from the 1920s were promoted as a home sun cure and emitted a large UVB share that burned the skin. Later commercial sunbeds, introduced in the late 1970s, used mostly UVA.[2]

In dermatology, a narrowband UVB fluorescent lamp emitting a peak around 311 to 312 nm (Philips TL-01) was reported in 1988 to be more effective for psoriasis than the TL-12 lamp in 10 patients, with longer tumour induction time in hairless mice.[6]

Dust blocks UV, and cleaning every 200 to 300 operating hours is described as typical. Skin oil on high-pressure bulbs can cause overheating and early failure. Broken lamps release mercury, and the page advises special precautions, especially for pregnant women.[1] Many US states restrict disposal of mercury-containing lamps.[1]

Case-control studies in the 1980s and 1990s examined sunbed and sunlamp use in relation to melanoma, including a 1990 study and a 1994 study in southern Sweden.[5][3] A 2005 study examined tanning beds, sunlamps and melanoma risk.[4] A nested case-control study in the Nurses' Health Study examined sun exposure and skin cancer risk.[7] A 1985 Montreal case-control study examined risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma.[8]

A laboratory study published in 2004 reported that UVB but not UVA radiation initiated melanoma in its experimental model.[9] A 2002 survey estimated use of indoor tanning sunlamps by US youth and their caregivers.[10]

sections.h: Use for appearance and tanning culture
paras: Sunlamps are used to produce a tan quickly and on a schedule, independent of weather or season. Wikipedia's indoor-tanning article says tanned skin was once a sign of leisure rather than a mark of low class from the 1920s onward, and that beds, booths and lamps are used in salons, gyms, spas and homes.[2] A 400-watt high-pressure lamp has been used as a face tanner, which is one reason the lamp form appears in face-focused discussions.[1]

UVA acts on existing pigment and UVB triggers new melanin production, which is why different lamp spectra give different looks of tan and different burn tendencies. Early 1920s home lamps with large UVB shares often burned, while later beds with about 95 percent UVA and 5 percent UVB were designed to tan more and burn less.[2] Sunless tanning products and bronzers are alternatives that achieve colour without UV; they are separate products and are not covered here.

Sun exposure has been used therapeutically since antiquity. The Faroese physician Niels Finsen, regarded as the father of modern phototherapy, treated lupus vulgaris with concentrated light from an artificial source and received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. [11] In the early 20th century Auguste Rollier and John Harvey Kellogg promoted sunlight treatment, and controlled trials by Dora Colebrook in the 1930s found it ineffective for the wide range of conditions it had been used for. [11]

Tanning lamps are either low-pressure phosphor-coated fluorescent tubes whose glass filters out UVC and whose phosphors convert short-wave UV to tanning wavelengths, or high-pressure quartz bulbs containing argon and mercury that need filter glass to block UVC. [1] Lamp life is typically hundreds to about 1,600 hours for low-pressure tubes, and output falls with age and temperature. [1] US lamps are labelled by their UVA to UVB ratio, which Wikipedia says does not indicate total output. [1]

sections.h: History of the sunlamp and tanning industry
paras: Finsen developed a carbon-arc UV lamp in 1890. Home sunlamps appeared in the 1920s and emitted a large proportion of UVB that caused burns, and Coco Chanel's 1923 tan helped make tanned skin fashionable. Friedrich Wolff developed beds emitting about 95 percent UVA and 5 percent UVB, with the sunbed invented in 1975 and the indoor tanning industry beginning in the US in 1978. [2]

The WHO's IARC classified UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Since 1997 many countries and US states have barred under-18s from indoor tanning, with France first; Brazil banned cosmetic tanning beds in 2009 and Australia banned commercial tanning in 2015. The FDA raised tanning beds to a moderate-risk device class in 2014 and requires a warning against use by under-18s. [2] Meta-analyses report 16 to 20 percent higher melanoma risk among indoor tanners, with higher figures for those who began young. [2]

sections.h: Appearance use and vitamin D claims
paras: Sunlamps are used to produce a tan, which people associate with a healthier or more attractive appearance, and some proponents promote UVB exposure for vitamin D. Wikipedia notes that some researchers say moderate tanning-bed use can be a vitamin D source, while most argue risks outweigh benefits and that supplements are adequate; the FTC held a seller's failure to disclose that tanning is unnecessary for vitamin D to be deceptive. [2]

The largest body of research on sunlamps concerns cancer risk. A 2005 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten studies (nine case-control and one cohort) found a summary odds ratio of 1.25 for melanoma among ever-users of sunlamps or sunbeds compared with never-users.[4] A 2021 meta-analysis of 36 melanoma studies and 18 non-melanoma skin cancer studies reported relative risks of 1.27 for melanoma, 1.40 for non-melanoma skin cancer and 1.58 for squamous cell carcinoma, with higher figures for early-onset cancers, first use at age 20 or younger, and ten or more sessions a year.[13]

A 2022 meta-analysis of five studies (1,753 uveal melanoma cases and 3,399 controls) reported a positive association between sunlamp use and uveal melanoma, an eye cancer.[12] Case-control work in Connecticut and an analysis of a 1991-1992 study examined who used sunbeds and sunlamps and their melanoma risk.[15][14] Wikipedia cites a 2012 analysis of 20 percent higher melanoma risk for ever-users and 59 percent higher for those starting before age 35.[2]

Researchers have also studied the mechanism. A 2004 Cancer Research study reported that UVB, but not UVA, initiated melanoma in its experimental model.[9] Surveys document use among young people: a 2002 Pediatrics survey estimated indoor tanning sunlamp use among US youth aged 11 to 18 and their caregivers, and an Italian study examined teenagers' awareness of sunbathing and sunlamp risks.[10][20]

Clinical phototherapy uses fluorescent UV lamps under supervision. Niels Finsen received the 1903 Nobel Prize for light treatment of lupus vulgaris, and Wikipedia describes UV light therapy as established for conditions including psoriasis, vitiligo and atopic dermatitis; narrowband UVB suits the face and neck in vitiligo.[11] Trials from the 1970s and 1980s examined fluorescent sunlamp bulbs for psoriasis: a 1979 study paired sunlamp exposure with tar gel, a 1981 study compared once-daily and twice-daily treatment, and a 1995 bilateral comparison of ten patients found no detectable difference between UVB with methoxsalen and UVB alone although all patients responded.[18][17][16]

The 1988 narrowband UVB study of Philips TL-01 lamps against TL-12 lamps is the best-known step toward modern medical lamps.[6] These supervised protocols are medical treatments for skin disease and differ from cosmetic tanning, which Wikipedia says is sometimes used as a substitute when clinic phototherapy is unavailable.[2]

In the United States the FDA classifies tanning beds as moderate-risk devices and requires a warning against use by under-18s, with many states adding age limits; Wikipedia reports the FDA's lamp tests are weighted toward UVB.[2][1] A 2011 Health Physics paper reports an ISO/CIE consensus on dose equivalence for the FDA's recommended maximum timer interval and exposure schedule.[19] Outside the US, Wikipedia notes bans on minors beginning with France in 1997, a Brazilian ban on cosmetic tanning beds in 2009, and an Australian ban on commercial tanning in 2015.[2] In 2016 the physician Joseph Mercola settled an FTC case over claims about tanning devices, with about 5.3 million dollars in refunds to purchasers.[2]

No intervention trials of home sunlamps as an appearance treatment were found. Related human research includes case-control studies and meta-analyses of sunbed and sunlamp use and melanoma, and small clinical comparisons of fluorescent UVB lamps in psoriasis.[4][13][16][17][18][6]

lore.intro: Sunlamps appear in tan-focused appearance discussion as an older, cheaper cousin of the tanning bed. The claims below are those commonly made by tanning proponents and historic heliotherapy promoters, set beside what research and regulators report.

claims.claim: A tan makes you look healthier and more attractive.
claims.believers: Tanning proponents associate a tan with health and attractiveness; Wikipedia places the tan fashion in the 1920s.[2]
claims.experts: The WHO classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen and public-health bodies advise against indoor tanning for appearance.[2]

claims.claim: Tanning lamps are a good vitamin D source.
claims.believers: Some proponents promote UVB exposure for vitamin D.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that most researchers argue skin cancer risk outweighs the benefit and that supplements are adequate; the FTC treated a seller's failure to disclose that tanning is unnecessary for vitamin D as deceptive.[2]

claims.claim: UVA-heavy lamps are safe because UVA does not burn.
claims.believers: Lamp makers shifted output to UVA after early burns.[2]
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis found elevated risk for indoor tanning overall, and a 2004 lab study reported UVB but not UVA initiated melanoma in its model, so the question of spectrum remains studied.[13][9]

claims.claim: Sunlamps can treat skin conditions at home.
claims.believers: Heliotherapy promoters of the early 20th century advocated sun and lamp treatment for many conditions.[11]
claims.experts: Controlled trials by Dora Colebrook in the 1930s found light therapy ineffective across the wide range it had been used for, while supervised UVB phototherapy is established for psoriasis and vitiligo.[11][16][17]

claims.claim: Unfiltered high-pressure bulbs are fine if you keep exposure short.
claims.believers: Owners of bare bulbs say a short exposure limits risk.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states unfiltered high-pressure bulbs emit dangerous UVC, require dichroic filter glass, and are illegal to operate unfiltered in salons.[1]

claims.claim: Sunlamps carry the same risks as other tanning devices.
claims.believers: Some users believe lamps are different from beds.
claims.experts: Meta-analyses pool sunbed and sunlamp use, finding higher melanoma risk, and a 2022 meta-analysis reported association with uveal melanoma.[4][12]
